brief.headlinerSide: On the headliner side Crumb is a mid-pack fit, not the leader: it ranks 4th of 9 in this pool, and Glass Beams (1st), Thee Sacred Souls (2nd) and Hermanos Gutiérrez (3rd) all rank above it on that side. The headliner-side-only tags (Funk, Groovy, Instrumental, Psychedelic Rock, Bass Guitar, Funky, Adventurous, Usa) describe the instrumental-groove surface Crumb does not lead on, while Crumb's own side-only tags versus the headliner (Dreamy, Ethereal, Saxophone, Youthful, Relationships, Dreams, Existentialism, Guitar) point to a softer, more vocal-and-dreamy register. So on this side it reads as adjacent rather than matching.
brief.targetSide: On the target side Crumb ranks 2nd of 9 — a high position but not the top one; Babe Rainbow ranks 1st there, so Crumb is not the strongest target-side act. Within this pool, Crumb shares Indie, Alternative Rock, Post Punk, Electronic, Guitar, Drums, Folk and Funk with the pooled target set (0.73 each), and it brings target-side-only tags Dreamy, Ethereal, Saxophone, Dreams, Laid-back, Youthful, Bass and Psychedelic Pop — the dreamy/psych-pop register the three reference artists are generally associated with. brief.answer: Take Crumb first. It is the balance pick, not the leader on either side: it ranks 2nd of 9 on the target side and 4th of 9 on the headliner side, a worst-side rank of 4, which is the lowest worst-side rank in this pool; the product rule (lowest worst-side rank, then rank sum) fixed it as priority. Concretely, Babe Rainbow outranks it on the target side (1st) and Glass Beams outranks it on the headliner side (1st), so neither side is where Crumb wins — it is where the two sides come closest to meeting without either ranking collapsing. Backups were likewise fixed by the rule: Babe Rainbow (target 1st, headliner 5th) and Thee Sacred Souls (headliner 2nd, target 5th); each has a worst-side rank of 5, looser than Crumb's 4, and they are lopsided in opposite directions. On the second question: the Qloo evidence supplied here compares the priority against the three reference artists as one pooled target set and gives no per-artist breakdown, so it cannot explain what separates Tame Impala listeners from Mac DeMarco listeners from Unknown Mortal Orchestra listeners. That difference is not answerable from this evidence and would need separate runs against each reference artist. Treat all of the above as taste affinity only — it is not ticket demand and does not show new audience growth, and booking fees, dates and willingness were checked outside this tool and are not claimed here.

brief.headlinerSide: On the Khruangbin side Men I Trust is a mid-pack, not a top, match. Its bass-forward, unhurried grooves and sparse arrangements sit nearer Khruangbin's instrumental groove space than most vocal-led acts on the shortlist, but on that side Glass Beams ranks closer to Khruangbin itself (instrumental, groove-led, texture-driven, no vocal centre), and Hermanos Gutiérrez also ranks closer (instrumental guitar duo in the same desert/Latin instrumental register). Thee Sacred Souls and Parcels rank at or above Men I Trust on pure groove. So the headliner-side case for Men I Trust is 'compatible', not 'strongest' — the strongest headliner-side names are Glass Beams and Hermanos Gutiérrez.
brief.targetSide: On the target side Men I Trust is the closest match to the bedroom-pop half of the reference set: hazy guitars, soft close-mic vocals and lo-fi-adjacent production that reads directly into Mac DeMarco's register and partly into Unknown Mortal Orchestra's psych-pop. It is not the closest to the psych-rock half: Crumb and Altin Gün rank closer to Tame Impala's guitar-and-synth psychedelia, and Tame Impala's big-room psych-pop scale is not something Men I Trust matches. The three reference artists are also not one audience — Tame Impala and UMO sit at a psych-rock/psych-pop pole while Mac DeMarco sits at a bedroom-pop pole, so any single support act will only touch part of the reference set.
brief.answer: Defensible pick: Men I Trust as priority, with Crumb and Parcels as backups. It is the one name on the shortlist that is closer to the bedroom-pop pole (Mac DeMarco, and partly UMO) while still carrying the bass-led, unhurried groove that Khruangbin's audience listens for — but be explicit that it loses on the headliner side to Glass Beams and Hermanos Gutiérrez, and loses on the psych-rock pole to Crumb and Altin Gün. If the team weights the Khruangbin instrumental-groove side more heavily, Glass Beams or Hermanos Gutiérrez is the honest headliner-side answer, at the cost of the bedroom-pop bridge; if it weights Tame Impala-style psych rock, Crumb or Altin Gün is the better lever. On the second question: yes, the three references can be explained, but as two poles rather than one audience — Tame Impala and Unknown Mortal Orchestra (psych rock / psych pop) versus Mac DeMarco (bedroom pop / lo-fi). That split is a taste and positioning reading, not a demand forecast, and no Qloo evidence is available in this version to quantify it.

evidence.claim: Khruangbin's audience is built around instrumental groove, dub/Thai-funk/soul texture and low-vocal, texture-led listening.
Tame Impala is psych rock/pop with synth-led production and a large festival-scale audience.
Mac DeMarco is bedroom pop / lo-fi jangle, small-scale and vocal-and-guitar centred.
Unknown Mortal Orchestra is psych pop with falsetto vocals and funk/soul undertones, sitting between a psych pole and a groove pole.
The three reference artists do not form one audience bloc: Tame Impala and UMO occupy a psych-rock/psych-pop pole, Mac DeMarco occupies a bedroom-pop pole.
Men I Trust is dream pop / bedroom pop with bass-forward, hazy production and soft vocals, with audience overlap toward Mac DeMarco-style bedroom pop and partly toward UMO.
Glass Beams is instrumental, groove-led and psychedelic, making it the closest shortlist act to Khruangbin on the headliner side, but it offers no vocal or bedroom-pop bridge.
Hermanos Gutiérrez is an instrumental guitar duo in a desert/Latin instrumental register — strong headliner-side texture, no bedroom-pop link.
Altin Gün is Turkish psych / Anatolian rock, ranking closer to the Tame Impala psych-rock pole than Men I Trust does.
Crumb is a psych-rock / dream-pop hybrid with jazz and synth elements, ranking closer to the psych-rock pole than Men I Trust while retaining dream-pop appeal.
Parcels is disco/funk groove with pop songwriting — strong on the groove side, weaker on the bedroom-pop side.
Bahamas (indie folk / soft rock) and Babe Rainbow (psych surf pop) sit outside the core of both poles on the shortlist as described.
